title: Ancient Nisa
kicker: Archaeology · 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE

blocks.tk: Aşgabatdan on sekiz kilometr günbatarda, Bagyr obasynyň ýanynda, Köpetdagyň eteginde iki gadymy depe bar. Olara Köne Nusaý we Täze Nusaý diýýärler. Iki depäniň arasy bir ýarym kilometr töweregi. 2007-nji ýylda bu ýer UNESKO-nyň Bütindünýä mirasynyň sanawyna girdi.
blocks.en: About 18 km west of Ashgabat, by the village of Bagyr at the foot of the Kopetdag, rise two ancient mounds, about a kilometre and a half apart: Old Nisa and New Nisa, Köne Nusaý and Täze Nusaý in Turkmen. In 2007 UNESCO put them on its World Heritage List as the Parthian Fortresses of Nisa.

blocks.tk: Iki müň ýyldan gowrak öň bu ýerde Parfiýa döwletiniň iň möhüm şäherleriniň biri bolupdyr. Parfiýa miladydan öňki üçünji asyrdan miladynyň üçünji asyryna çenli uly döwlet bolupdyr we Rim bilen göreşipdir. Bu sebit atlary bilen meşhurdy. Köne Nusaý galadyr: onuň daşynda beýik diwar we kyrkdan gowrak diň bar eken. Adamlaryň köpüsi Täze Nusaýda ýaşapdyr. Täze Nusaýyň diwarlary dokuz metre çenli beýik eken.
blocks.en: More than two thousand years ago this was one of the earliest and most important cities of the Parthian empire, which, in UNESCO's words, was a major power from the mid-3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE and a rival of Rome; the region was famous for its horses. Old Nisa, a citadel of 14 hectares ringed by an earthen rampart with more than forty towers, was a royal and ceremonial centre; most people lived in New Nisa, a town with walls up to 9 m high, according to the ICOMOS evaluation.

blocks.tk: Arheologlar Nusaýda müňlerçe ýazgyly küýze bölegini tapypdyrlar. Ýazgylaryň birinde galanyň köne ady bar eken: Mitradatkert, ýagny “Mitradatyň galasy”. Alymlaryň pikirine görä, bu at patyşa Birinji Mitradatyň adyndan gelýär. Beýleki ýazgylarda patyşanyň ekin meýdanlary we üzüm baglary barada habarlar bar eken.
blocks.en: Archaeologists have found some 2,700 inscribed potsherds at Nisa. One of them gives the citadel's ancient name: Mithradatkert, “the fortress of Mithradates”, which scholars connect with King Mithradates I, who ruled from about 171 to 138 BCE. Other sherds record the produce of the royal farms and vineyards.

blocks.tk: Gazuw işleri 1930-njy ýyllarda başlapdyr. Ikinji jahan urşundan soň M. E. Massonyň ýolbaşçylygyndaky ekspedisiýa bu ýerde köp ýyl işläpdir. 1948-nji ýylyň güýzünde arheologlar “Inedördül jaýda” ajaýyp zatlary tapypdyrlar: pil süňkünden ritonlar. Ritonlar şah ýaly uzyn içgi gaplarydyr. Olaryň aşagynda ganatly arslanlaryň, kentawrlaryň we beýleki jandarlaryň şekilleri bar. Olaryň ýokarky böleginde grek hudaýlarynyň şekilleri hem bar.
blocks.en: Excavations began in the 1930s. After the Second World War the South Turkmenistan Archaeological Complex Expedition, led by M. E. Masson, worked here for many years and made Nisa one of the great digs of Soviet Central Asia. In the autumn of 1948, in the building now called the Square House, the team found a group of rhytons: horn-shaped drinking vessels carved from elephant ivory, ending in figures such as winged lion-griffins and centaurs, with friezes of Greek gods. Encyclopaedia Iranica counts about forty of them.

blocks.tk: Şol ýyl Aşgabatdaky güýçli ýer titremesi ritonlara hem zeper ýetirdi. Soňra alymlar olary dikeldipdirler we birnäçe muzeýe paýlapdyrlar. Häzir olaryň käbiri Moskwadaky muzeýlerde. Ritonlaryň ýaşy barada alymlaryň pikiri dürli: käbirleriniň pikirine görä, olar miladydan öňki üçünji asyrdan galypdyr, beýlekileriň pikirine görä, has soňky döwürden. Megerem, patyşalar dabaralarda olardan şerap içendirler.
blocks.en: The great Ashgabat earthquake of 1948 damaged them; they were later restored and divided among several museums, some of them in Moscow. Their date is debated: Iranica's article on rhytons places them in the 3rd century BCE, its article on Nisa in the 2nd or 1st century BCE. So is their use. They were probably drinking and libation vessels for feasts and ceremonies, perhaps royal ones, but, as Iranica notes, the context in which they were used is not known.

blocks.tk: Köne Nusaýda başga syrlar hem köp. Uly tegelek zal näme bolupdyr: ybadathana, kümmet ýa-da başga bir zat? Alymlar entek muny anyk bilmeýärler. Italiýaly arheologlar türkmen alymlary bilen bu ýerde 1990-njy ýyldan bäri işleýärler. Gadymy bir taryhçynyň ýazgysyna görä, bu ýerde Parfiýa patyşalarynyň mazarlary bolupdyr, ýöne olary entek hiç kim tapmandyr. Häzir syýahatçylar bu ýere gelýärler we gadymy palçyk diwarlaryň arasynda gezýärler.
blocks.en: Other questions remain open. The great Round Hall, 17 m across, may have been a temple, a mausoleum or a shrine to heroes: its purpose, the nomination file says, has not been established. Italian archaeologists from Turin have worked here with Turkmen colleagues since 1990. The ancient geographer Isidore of Charax wrote of royal tombs at Nisa, but they have not been found. Today visitors walk among the mud-brick walls of Old Nisa, much of which is still unexcavated.

blocks.title: Reading the Turkmen
blocks.text: Nobody alive saw Parthian Nisa, so its history is told in `-(Y)pdYr`: *bolupdyr*, *ýaşapdyr*, *tapypdyrlar*. What the finds reveal comes with *eken*: *diň bar eken*. And the guess about the kings is `-dYr`: *içendirler*, they must have drunk.

questions.q: When were the fortresses of Nisa put on UNESCO's World Heritage List?
questions.explain: 1948 is when the rhytons were found, and the 1930s when excavations began.

questions.q: What are the Nisa rhytons made of?
questions.explain: *pil süňkünden ritonlar*: rhytons of ivory, literally of elephant bone.

questions.q: Why does the text say *içendirler* about the kings?
options: It's a guess: they must have drunk from them.
They drank from them every day.
questions.explain: *Megerem* and `-An` + `-dYr`: a confident guess, since the rhytons' use is not known.

sources.title: Parthian Fortresses of Nisa
sources.note: Inscribed in 2007 on criteria (ii) and (iii); the Parthian empire a major power from the mid-3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE and a rival of Rome; at the foot of the Kopet-Dag

sources.title: Nisa (Turkmenistan), No 1242: ICOMOS evaluation
sources.note: Bagyr settlement, Akhal; Old Nisa a 14 ha tell with a rampart of more than 40 towers; New Nisa a 25 ha tell 1.5 km north-west, where most people lived; Mithradatkert named on one of 2,700 ostraka, after Mithradates I; excavations since 1930; the Round Hall, 17 m across, as temple, mausoleum or heroon not yet established

sources.title: Nisa
sources.note: About 18 km west of Ashgabat, west and east of the village of Bagir; YuTAKE under M. E. Masson after the war; the Square House and its treasury; the rhytons with winged lion-griffins, centaurs and friezes of the Olympian gods, probably 2nd–1st century BCE, their context of use unknown; the royal tombs mentioned by Isidore of Charax not found

sources.title: Rhyton
sources.note: Forty large carved ivory rhyta of the 3rd century BCE found in Soviet excavations at Old Nisa (Mithridatkert), made from elephant ivory
